title: Hannibal Rising
full_review:
Psychopaths -- like heroes -- are made, not born. So suggests "Hannibal Rising" (MGM), the bland, brutal prequel to "Silence of the Lambs" that disconcertingly blurs the distinction between homicide and heroism.

Based on Thomas Harris' fourth novel about serial killer Hannibal "the Cannibal" Lecter -- portrayed by Anthony Hopkins in the 1991 thriller and two subsequent films -- the new installment follows Hannibal from his childhood in Nazi-occupied Lithuania through early adulthood, tracing his descent from traumatized youth to mass murderer.

Opening scenes detail how an orphaned Hannibal (played by Aaron Thomas) is forced to witness an unspeakable crime involving his little sister, Mischa (Helena-Lia Tachovaska), and a gang of ravenous Nazi collaborators -- led by the feral Grutas (Rhys Ifans) -- that sets the boy on his deranged future path.

Most of the film, however, involves a teenage Hannibal (now matured into French newcomer Gaspard Ulliel), who -- after escaping a Soviet orphanage and attending medical school in Paris -- tracks down and sadistically kills Mischa's murderers.
The movie also allows Hannibal a romance with a Japanese widow, Lady Murasaki (Gong Li), who takes him in and educates him in the way of the sword.

"Silence" -- though dealing with a similarly lurid subject matter -- was a smart and stylish psychological thriller. Director Peter Weber's new movie, conversely, is a standard revenge drama with a patina of respectability.

The script, written by Harris, merely moves from one gruesome killing to the next, without ever delving into the complexities of Hannibal's character or exploring the nature of evil.

Unlike Hopkins, whose hypnotic intensity made Hannibal mesmerizing to watch, Ulliel, despite mimicking some of the British actor's mannerisms, is colorless.

Whereas Hopkins was unambiguously sinister, what's most troubling here is how audiences are asked to root for the burgeoning serial killer, positioning him as a hero of sorts by pitting him against Nazi thugs.

"Quid pro quo" -- "something for something" -- Hopkins' Hannibal was fond of saying. Here all you get for your money is two hours of exploitative ugliness.

The film contains much bloody and sadistic violence, revenge themes with vigilante justice, grisly images including a decapitation, suggested cannibalism, some crude sexual references and a few instances of rough language. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
